output:
*Interview with Bastien Girard, établisseur, of Le Locle, in the dining room. Taken down by the inspector in the early hours of 1 January 1900.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Girard, please sit down. I know this is a hard hour for everyone in the house. Take your time.

GIRARD: Hard. It's a terrible thing. Aurèle dead, and we were at his table this evening drinking to the new century. I can't make it true yet.

MATTHEY: Let us go back to the evening, if you can. You were at dinner with the household.

GIRARD: Yes. Monnier did his usual thing with the watches. Every year he makes us take them out and tells each man what is wrong with his. I would not show him mine.

MATTHEY: Why was that?

GIRARD: Because I buy and sell movements, Inspector, and a merchant does not hand his watch to a man who wants to lecture him about it in front of his guests. And there was the business of the repeater. He wanted to sell me the rights to the thing he has been making. I offered a fair price. He wanted more for the name as well. We quarrelled about it at the table, and I'll admit I raised my voice.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

GIRARD: After dinner I sat on alone in the dining room with the brandy. I heard the temple strike ten while I sat there. I did not look at my watch. I didn't want the time. I wanted to be left alone with my glass.

MATTHEY: You did not look at your watch then.

GIRARD: No. Later I went out into the street to smoke. It was twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch. It is cold enough up here to take the skin off your face. I had one of my Brissago, the cheap ones. I can't afford anything better this year, and I smoke them anyway because I don't care what a cigar tastes like when I'm thinking. I stayed under the front windows of the house.

MATTHEY: Why under the front windows?

GIRARD: I walk in the cold to think. I was thinking about the repeater, and about Félix. I'll say it plainly. The boy owes me money, a good deal of it, and he has been avoiding me. I wasn't going to press him tonight.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything from the house while you were smoking?

GIRARD: The piano started up in the salon just as I lit my cigar. It was twenty-nine minutes past ten by my watch. I know nothing about music, but it sounded well played to me.

MATTHEY: Go on.

GIRARD: At twenty-six minutes to eleven by my watch I heard faint, quick bells from the master's window up above. That's all I can tell you about them. I made nothing of them at the time. A man in my trade hears a dozen small noises a day and does not stop to ask what each one is.

MATTHEY: You went back into the house after that.

GIRARD: I did. I came back in at fourteen minutes to eleven by my watch. The hall clock had just struck eleven, and its face showed two minutes past eleven. That is the old Morbier clock by the stairs. I went straight up to Félix in the library.

MATTHEY: You went to the library, not to the atelier.

GIRARD: To the library. Félix was there. We talked about his debts, and I'll not pretend it was a pleasant talk.

MATTHEY: You have a poor opinion of Dr Vauthier. Is that right?

GIRARD: I don't care for his company. He quotes Latin to make a man feel small, and he is always at Odile's elbow, always the family friend. I have never liked a man who plays cards so well and talks so easily about other people's health.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about the evening you have not yet told me?

GIRARD: Only that I would have shown the master my watch if I had known what was coming. I'd have let him tell me everything wrong with it. I'd have given him that much.
